national.summary: At least 20 flights in Europe deal with bomb threats, adding to what one expert calls an unusual level of hoaxes in a short time period, suggesting "a very deliberate act."
national.body: Paris — At least 20 commercial flights in Europe had to deal with bomb threats Thursday, with at least one being diverted to a military base in France. While authorities have reported no explosives discovered on any of the jets, and they all appeared to be hoaxes, Thursday's incidents add to a fast-growing number of journeys hit by similar threats this week, which one expert said suggested a "very deliberate act." British authorities dismissed threats to about seven flights earlier this week as hoaxes, but the number of impacted journeys soared to at least 27 on Thursday, meaning significant disruption for thousands of passengers and raising concerns about a possible coordinated effort to impact travel on the continent. At least two more European flights, along with several Irish and British news outlets, got similar threats on Friday.No authorities have confirmed a link between any of the threats, but Spanish Foreign Minister Jose Manuel Albares said Friday that Europe appeared to be facing "hybrid aggression and a form of psychological warfare."David Kaminski-Morrow, Air Transport Editor with FlightGlobal, declined to speculate on who might be behind the threats to commercial flights this week, but he noted that "we currently live in a time of political aggression in regions including Europe, and it's a pretty effective tactic if someone is looking to cause disruption.""The cluster of threats seems unusual, but it's hard to determine the extent to which they might be organized," he said, noting that "the publicity alone could spur further threats unrelated to earlier ones."Kaminski-Morrow noted that, under an international aviation convention in place for more than 80 years, the pilot in command of a flight has the final authority over its safety, "and airlines always take threats to safety seriously. national.title: What to know about Pope Leo XIV's trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru
national.summary: Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru.
national.body:
VATICAN CITY (AP) — Pope Leo XIV is returning home to the continent where he spent two decades as a missionary priest and learned to be a pastor, visiting Uruguay, Argentina and his second homeland of Peru.

The Nov. 6-17 trip marks the longest and farthest of his papacy and is coming just three weeks after Leo underwent surgery Oct. 13 to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Doctors nevertheless gave him the green light to make the trip.

Latin America still is home to around 40% of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics, but the Catholic proportion of the region's population has shrunk in recent year s and the decreases are especially notable in the countries Leo will visit.

The trip begins in Uruguay, whose secular identity and separation of church and state are so deeply entrenched that Christmas is officially "Family Day" and Holy Week is "Tourism Week."

According to Vatican statistics, nearly 77% of Uruguay's 3.5 million people are baptized Catholics. But more than half of all Uruguayans identify as religiously unaffiliated — the highest portion in Latin America – and only a fraction of those who identify as Catholic actually go to Mass regularly.

Leo's itinerary includes a stop at a parish in Casavalle, a poor neighborhood on the outskirts of Montevideo plagued by drug trafficking and gang violence. The church works with national and municipal authorities on support initiatives, including housing construction and addiction recovery programs.

Leo will also celebrate Mass in Paysandú, some 375 kilometers (230 miles) from the capital and chosen because of its accessibility to those living north of the Río Negro, a river that crosses the country, and proximity to the Argentine city of Colón.

The visit begins with a welcome ceremony at the Plaza Independencia in the center of Montevideo, a symbol of Uruguay's national identity and history. The plaza features a monument to independence hero José Gervasio Artigas.

national.title: AI stocks climb after trillions wiped from market values
national.summary: Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat election victory would mean slower AI development.
national.body:
Shares in artificial intelligence and technology firms have been climbing following an enormous sell-off that wiped trillions of dollars off stock values.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq stock index opened higher following a market rout that began in the US on Thursday before spilling over to Asian and European markets into Friday.

Investors had been selling off tech shares in part due to concerns the Democrat victory in the midterm elections would mean slower artificial intelligence development.

However the latest US employment figures added to a mixed picture for American markets on Friday morning, with an unexpectedly strong 165,000 jobs added to the economy in September.

On Thursday, businesses closely linked to artificial intelligence development took a hammering on stock markets, particularly chip and semiconductor makers.

But the Nasdaq Composite opened up on Friday and flattened out around 1.7% higher by lunchtime, reversing some of its 5.5% fall.

The S&P 500, which tracks the share prices of the largest publicly-traded US companies, was around 0.9% higher by lunchtime. The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened a little down before nudging into positive territory.

Nvidia, which shed hundreds of billions in market value on Thursday after shares slid more than 9%, began Friday up more than 6% but settled around 4% higher as trading continued.

national.title: Dozens of Democrats eyeing 2028 presidential run, says former Obama aide
national.summary: Jim Messina tells the BBC that after Democrats' midterm victories he's talked to "over two dozen campaigns", with some already hiring staff.
national.body:
More than two dozen Democrats are eyeing runs for the White House in 2028, following their party's success in the US midterm elections this week, according to the man behind Barack Obama's successful re-election bid.

Jim Messina, who led Obama's 2012 campaign, said that since Democrats saw major victories in congressional races as well as state elections, he's spoken to "over two dozen campaigns" that are actively considering running in 2028 and have begun the financing process and hiring staff.

"I think you're going to start having Democrats announce exploratory committees next week or the next couple of weeks, probably after Thanksgiving", Messina told the BBC's Americast podcast.

He said he already knows someone relocating to work on a governor's presidential campaign.

He also predicted that the number could shrink as candidates faced pressure to raise large sums needed for the primary contests that will decide the party's nominee.

Messina gave some insight into the conversations he's had, saying: "When I sit down with candidates or their campaigns, I say to them, 'Tell me your economic vision for the future of this country. What are you going to do on AI?'"

Then there's another factor: the outgoing president, Donald Trump, who will still be in office during the campaign season.

"And so, do the Democrats take the bait and talk about Donald Trump every day, or do you stay focused on your message?" he said.

national.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq edged up in early trading after a Thursday rout driven by concerns about a potential slowdown in data center construction.
national.body: Stocks showed signs of life as U.S. financial markets opened on Friday, stabilizing after a steep selloff the previous day driven by concerns over a potential slowdown in data center construction. In early trading, the S&P 500 climbed 72 points, or nearly 1%, erasing losses after it suffered its worst day since April 2025 on Thursday. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite rose 437 points, or 1.8%, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 129 points, or 0.2%. Markets soared immediately after the midterm elections earlier this week, but quickly reversed course on Thursday as investors assessed whether sweeping Democratic victories could lead to tighter restrictions on building data centers and weaker spending on artificial intelligence. As of Friday, voters had approved more than 40 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across the country, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting.Tech stocks started to recover on Friday, helping pull the Nasdaq higher after a brutal beating on Thursday that caused the index to shed more than 1,400 points and enter a "correction," or when stocks fall at least 10% from their previous peak. Chipmaker Nvidia — a bellwether for the AI sector — gained 6.6% in early trading, and semiconductor manufacturer Micron Technology rose 9.8%.The so-called hyperscalers — the companies leading the data center buildout — saw modest gains in early trading, with Google-owner Alphabet climbing 2%, Amazon up 1.1% and Meta gaining 2.4%; Microsoft shed 0.6%.Slowing AI investment?A key question for Wall Street is whether AI companies will deliver the revenue growth investors are banking on. national.summary: Democrats won sizable House and Senate majorities in the 2026 midterm elections, but the exact margins are unclear because some races haven't been projected yet. Here's where the results stand.
national.body: Washington — The makeup of Congress shifted dramatically in the 2026 midterm elections, as Democrats decisively won control of the Senate and picked up dozens of House seats — in what's on track to be one of the largest midterm routs in recent decades.The exact margins of Congress are not yet clear, as winners have not yet been projected in two Senate races and more than two dozen House races. They include GOP-held districts with razor-thin margins, a few Democratic seats that could flip to Republicans and several races in California and other Western states that still need to count ballots.Here's a look at the congressional races that CBS News has not yet projected, including where the results stand:Senate Toss-UpsDemocrats are set to enter next year with at least 54 Senate seats, compared to Republicans' 44. Two Senate races still haven't been called — one has long been viewed as a battleground, and the other came out of nowhere.Alaska Senate: Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan is running for reelection against Democrat Mary Peltola, a razor-thin race rocked by a last-minute scandal over how another Dan Sullivan got on the ballot. The count could drag on due to both outstanding ballots and Alaska's ranked choice voting system, which allows voters to rank candidates in order of preference. If no candidate is the top choice of a majority of voters, the last-place candidate is eliminated and the counting process moves to a second round. Final results aren't expected until 15 days after Election Day. Both the Sullivan and Peltola campaigns have argued they have the upper hand.Mississippi Senate: The race between GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and Democrat Scott Colom was not widely expected to be competitive, but it remains a toss-up. State officials say thousands of mail ballots are outstanding and can legally arrive within five days of the election, and there are an unknown number of "affidavit" ballots from voters whose eligibility needs to be checked. Colom and Hyde-Smith have both predicted that they'll emerge victorious.Democrats on DefenseThe dozens of red districts that Democrats flipped were the primary story of Tuesday night, but a few Republican House candidates are still trying to swim against the tide, either due to redistricting or a favorable local political makeup.Maine's 2nd District: This red, pro-Trump district is one of Republicans' top opportunities

national.title: Trump's Washington projects are a likely casualty as Democrats claim Congress
national.summary: The work his administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to encounter far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.
national.body:
Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press Lisa Mascaro, Associated Press

WASHINGTON (AP) — In his first public appearance after an election that soundly repudiated his policies, President Donald Trump turned to a topic both familiar and, given the context, surprising: not his policies or politics but his efforts to remake pieces of the city that is the backdrop to his presidency.

Despite Trump's affinity for project management, though, with Democrats taking control of Congress, the work his administration is doing to change the physical face of the District of Columbia is sure to encounter far more roadblocks than it did for the first two years of his second term.

From the renaming of and renovation plans for the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and erecting an arch 100 feet (30.48 meters) taller than the Statue of Liberty without its pedestal, Trump has been deeply involved in how D.C. looks. Democrats have voiced opposition but, in terms of power, have been in the wilderness.

The potential collision point between opposition oversight from Democrats and the Republican president's preoccupation with the projects was evident in his last message to the American public before the election — and in his first afterward, too.

Both focused to some degree on his projects. On Monday, it was the reflecting pool in front of the Lincoln Memorial ; on Wednesday, it was a tour of the under-construction White House ballroom , where he talked columns and steel beams and Corinthian designs.

Jared Huffman of California, the top Democrat on the Natural Resources Committee with jurisdiction over the Interior Department that is involved with operations at parks and federal lands, spent much of the past year probing and questioning Trump's projects, laying the groundwork for this moment.

national.title: Could the US midterms burst the AI bubble?
national.summary: Fears of more AI regulation appear to have sparked fear among investors, but concerns about the industry have been growing for some time.
national.body:
Is the artificial intelligence (AI) gold rush coming to an end, or is this simply a reality check?

That's the question which is hanging over investors, and which has prompted steep falls on the world's stock markets.

The sell-off in the US on Thursday was most dramatic on the Nasdaq, home to tech industry titans such as Alphabet, Nvidia, Meta and Apple.

It followed sweeping gains by the Democrats in this week's mid-term elections in the US, which have given the party full control of Congress.

A number of leading Democrats campaigned against the unhindered expansion of data centres, which have underpinned the growth of artificial intelligence.

Fears this will lead to more regulation of AI appear to have sparked fear among investors. But concerns about the industry's prospects have been growing for some time.

The release of Chat GPT by Open AI in late 2022 is widely seen as having generated massive public and corporate interest in the practical uses of AI. It also sparked a modern-day gold rush.

Investors flocked to put their money into companies producing computer chips and networking infrastructure, building data centres and providing the energy to power them, as well as developing the AI itself. The value of tech companies soared.

Ballots are still being counted in the US midterm elections but the political landscape is already pivoting to the 2028 White House race.

Buoyed by major gains in Congress, Democrats will have momentum as they prepare for the contest to succeed President Donald Trump.

But a good showing in the midterms does not guarantee a White House win two years later. Barack Obama was re-elected in 2012 despite huge Republican gains in 2010.

No one has yet entered the presidential race but potential candidates will be preparing behind the scenes.

Vice-President's JD Vance's reflection on where the midterms went wrong for Republicans has been interpreted as him paving the way for a 2028 run.

The results of Tuesday's election and the historic size of Democratic gains could shape the White House race in several ways.

Several prominent potential presidential candidates were running in the 2026 midterms - and some emerged looking strong.

Georgia Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff won by a sizeable margin in the politically competitive state that Trump won in 2024.

national.summary: The estranged father of Meghan Markle was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material, two people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.
national.body:
Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press Alanna Durkin Richer, Associated Press

Meghan Markle's father was arrested Friday morning by federal agents in Florida on charges related to child sexual abuse material, two people familiar with the matter told The Associated Press.

Thomas Markle Sr. was arrested outside Tampa, according to the people who were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation and spoke on the condition of anonymity.

His arrest follows reports by The Sun, a British tabloid newspaper, that Meghan's half brother found a collection of child sexual abuse images while clearing out the home of their father in the Philippines.

Meghan Markle, the wife of Prince Harry, recently said she was "deeply distressed" by allegations that a collection of child sexual abuse images had been found at her father's former home. She also revealed that a letter containing "troubling allegations" about him had been sent to London police in 2018.

"It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated," Meghan said of the letter. "I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications' distortion over the years, any distance from my father and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children was for one reason: to protect them."

Meghan, an American citizen who starred in the U.S. television drama "Suits," married Harry at Windsor Castle in 2018. They have two children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet.

Her father, a retired television lighting and photography director, did not attend the wedding, prompting extensive coverage in the British media of Meghan's estrangement from her father.

national.summary: See the maps and charts that show how America voted in the US midterm elections.
national.body:
It's been an extraordinary night for the Democrats in the US midterms.

They have taken control of the Senate and the House of Representatives too.

The results in the Senate are beyond what the Democrats would have expected. North Carolina was a likely pick-up but the previously deep red state of South Carolina was a huge shock and Kansas had not returned a Democratic senator since 1932.

Texas , Iowa , Ohio and Maine also turned blue and the Democrats held Michigan . There are two seats remaining, Alaska and Mississippi , both are on a knife edge.

The shift from Republican to Democrat happened across the country. Some of the biggest swings since the presidential election in 2024 were in Texas where the Democrats took the Senate seat and the governor. Several counties on the state's southern border swung by more that 50 percentage points.

The BBC's partner CBS News projected the Democrats would win the House just after 03:00 GMT on Wednesday (22:00 EST Tuesday).

Now it's a question of how big that win will be as counting continues.

Two significant seats are Florida 14 and Florida 25 which the Democrats have held. This is a blow to the Republicans' attempt to redraw the boundaries in their favour.

national.title: Musk says Tesla will end Cybertruck production next year
national.summary: Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the electric car maker will halt production of its Cybertruck next year and prioritize self-driving taxis.
national.body: Tesla's Cybertruck has reached the end of the road. Elon Musk announced on X Friday that the electric car maker would wind down production of its stainless-steel pickup truck at its Texas factory by mid-2027. Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, said the move is to "make room for increased Cybercab production," referring to Tesla's self-driving taxi.Wall Street analyst Dan Ives, senior managing director of Yorkville Ives & Co, told CBS News in an email that "the writing was on the wall" for the Cybertruck given the vehicle's high price and subpar demand. Tesla first unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019, capturing attention for its boxy design and futuristic look. Tesla touted the car as a rolling fortress that could tow 14,000 pounds and withstand hits from sledgehammers and even firearms. But the vehicle has been beset by quality problems and has faced numerous recalls. It's unclear if production of the Cybertruck will continue at other factories, although it appears unlikely. According to Forbes, Tesla's gigafactory in Texas is the only one that currently manufactures the pickup.Tesla sold only 20,237 Cybertrucks in 2025, down from 38,965 the previous year, according to figures from Kelley Blue Book. After commercial production of the truck started in 2023, Musk had predicted annual sales of 250,000 Cybertrucks. The vehicle initially sold for $60,990. Cybertrucks also became a flashpoint in the debate over Musk's role in the Trump administration as the head of the Department of Government Efficiency. In a sign of protest, some people vandalized Cybertrucks at Tesla dealerships."Musk is focused on robotics and the robotaxi era, which frees up production with the Cybertruck ramp now winding down," Ives said.Tesla unveiled its Cybercab, a two-seat vehicle with no steering wheel or pedals, in 2024. Production of the vehicle began at the company's Texas plant in April, and service began in Austin in September.

national.title: Jay Rockefeller, former West Virginia governor and U.S. senator, dies at 89
national.summary: Rockefeller came from one of the nation's richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states.
national.body:
CHARLESTON, W.Va. (AP) — Jay Rockefeller, the last member of his family's political dynasty — and the only Democrat — who served as West Virginia's governor and later a longtime U.S. senator, has died. He was 89.

Rockefeller died Thursday night at his home in Washington, said Mary Stewart, vice president for external affairs at WETA, the public broadcasting station where Rockefeller's wife, Sharon, serves as president and CEO.

Rockefeller came from one of the nation's richest families to spend a half century in public service in one of the poorest states. He arrived in 1964 as a worker in an anti-poverty program, was elected governor a dozen years later and served two terms, then spent 30 years as a U.S. senator.

"I could not imagine a more rewarding career," Rockefeller said upon his retirement in 2015.

He was born John D. Rockefeller IV in New York City. His great-grandfather, Standard Oil Co. founder John Rockefeller, died a month before Rockefeller's birth. His father, John D. Rockefeller III, was a well-known philanthropist. Uncles Winthrop (Arkansas) and Nelson (New York) were Republican governors. Another uncle, David Rockefeller, ran Chase Manhattan Bank.

A few years out of college at age 27, Rockefeller moved to the West Virginia mining community of Emmons to participate in the Volunteers in Service to America program, a time that Rockefeller said proved transformative.

"It explains every policy I pursued and every vote I have cast. It was where my beliefs were bolted down, and where my passions met my principles," he said in an emotional farewell speech from the Senate floor on Dec. 4, 2014.

While he intended for his stay in the state to be brief, Rockefeller broke from his family's Republican tradition and was elected to the state House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. By combining money with hard work in a traditionally Democratic state, Rockefeller overcame suspicions of political opportunism and rose from state legislator to secretary of state to governor.

national.title: Two dead after bus crashes in France, officials say
national.summary: One child and one young adult were killed in the crash, local authorities say, with more injured.
national.body:
A young girl and an 18-year-old man have died after a bus crashed in eastern France, local authorities have said.

The bus was travelling between Lyon and Bourg-en-Bresse when it crashed at around 07:00 local time on Friday in the town of Lent.

The bus was carrying 43 passengers, including 15 children, the Bourg-en-Bresse prosecutor's office said. Three people are in a critical condition and at least 13 others have sustained minor injuries.

French President Emmanuel Macron said his thoughts were with the victims, the injured, and their families.

In a post on X, he said the nation stood by their side and thanked the rescue teams involved.

The town's mayor Yves Cristin told French media the bus "left the road and hit a tree in the ditch".

The two people killed have been identified by authorities. However, there have been differing reports as to the age of the girl.

The prosecutor's office said it was "opening an investigation into the incident, on charges of road homicide and aggravated road traffic injuries".

national.title: Judge blocks construction of Trump's massive arch after federal agency approval
national.summary: The Trump administration had hoped the construction of the 250-foot arch could begin as early as this week.
national.body:
A federal judge has temporarily blocked construction of US President Donald Trump's "triumphal arch" in the nation's capital.

US District Judge Tanya Chutkan ruled that there should be a 14-day pause before any work can start on the arch in Washington which the Trump administration had said could begin this week.

Earlier on Thursday the National Capital Planning Commission (NCPC) voted 8-4 to allow construction of the planned 250ft (72m) arch.

Trump appointees on the board said the arch would be a fitting tribute to US history and to veterans but opponents have argued it would block the view of Arlington National Cemetery, the resting place of thousands of US soldiers and service people.

The so-called Arc de Trump - a play on the name of the famous arch in Paris, the Arc de Triomphe - is one of the president's efforts to remake the capital city in his style and is meant to commemorate the country's 250th anniversary.

The approval on Thursday evening came after nearly nine hours of public comment.

"The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission's decision to fully approve President Trump's historic vision to build a much needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, DC," a White House spokesperson told the BBC in a statement.

It is not yet clear when construction of the arch could begin, as several lawsuits seek to block the project.

national.title: New wave of bomb threats hit European airlines
national.summary: No link has been established between the threats against the airlines and those against the media outlets.
national.body:
European airlines have again been hit with a new wave of bomb threats - in the third such incident this week.

On Friday multiple flights to and from Lisbon, Rome, Prague and Sofia were targeted and the threats saw three planes escorted by Hungarian fighter jets, authorities said.

It also saw a number of high-profile media organisations, including Ireland's public broadcaster RTÉ , evacuated after threats were made against them - although there has been no concrete links between the messages against airlines and the broadcasters.

The disruption comes after nearly 30 aircraft and several airports across Europe were impacted by threats earlier this week , in what the UK called a "malicious hoax".

Published 4 hours ago A Ryanair flight scheduled to leave Lisbon for Rome on Friday was targeted with a threat, the airline said, while at least 11 flights were targeted in the Czech Republic and Bulgaria, according to AFP.

France also reported at least four of its flights were targeted by threats, however they all landed safely.

As airlines were dealing with this latest wave of threats, several media outlets, including RTÉ, were evacuated after similar warnings were made against them.

Staff at the Irish Independent newspaper and the Dublin offices of radio stations NewstalkFM and TodayFM, were also advised to leave their buildings and UK broadcaster Sky said it also received a security threat.

national.title: European air traffic is targeted by new threats after a week of hoaxes
national.summary: Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Two broadcasters also received security threats.
national.body:
Passengers arrive at the Henri Coanda International Airport pass under a Schengen Information sign, in Otopeni, near Bucharest, Romania, on March 31, 2024. Andreea Alexandru/AP hide caption

BERLIN — Officials across Europe reported a fresh slew of bomb threats against multiple flights on Friday, following a string of hoaxes that have caused flight diversions this week. Two broadcasters also received security threats.

No suspicious items were found and no one was injured, but the threats have raised concern because they came as Europe digests other recent disruptions — including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.

Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation across the continent, according to the European air traffic authority. Eurocontrol said it was aware of bomb threats against 14 flights on Thursday — only 0.05% of all of the nearly 26,300 flights across the European network that day — and seven on Tuesday.

In Hungary, the defense minister said military fighter jets escorted three separate passenger planes Friday across the country's airspace within an hour after each received bomb threats. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said they were flights from Brussels to Sofia and from Prague to Cyprus and Romania.

Law From comedian to convicted rapist: What to know about Russell Brand French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office said Friday that "four new bomb threats were made today against aircraft flying over French territory." The planes landed safely at Paris' Orly Airport and bomb disposal experts were conducting inspections. The office didn't give details of the flights affected.

Other incidents included threats against a Prague to Bucharest flight operated by Romanian carrier Tarom, and a Ryanair flight traveling from Lisbon to Rome. A WizzAir flight from Prague to Rome was diverted to Venice after a bomb alert, and passengers were evacuated after the aircraft landed.

Security inspections were carried out and no explosives were found.

national.title: Tanzanian opposition leader found guilty of inciting unrest but acquitted of treason
national.summary: The 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, says the charges are politically motivated.
national.body:
Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country.

A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge.

But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election.

Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated.

The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement.

"By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Lissu said he had only been charged with treason, not incitement.

"The offence of incitement is one that you, honourable judges, have manufactured. You have created an offence that did not exist, and you have done so on political directives," Lissu told the court.

national.title: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult is sentenced to 200 years in prison
national.summary: Cult leader Paul Mackenzie was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.
national.body:
Good News International Church pastor Paul Mackenzie, who has been convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult, awaits his sentence at the Mombasa High Court in Mombasa, Kenya, Friday. Brian Inganga/AP hide caption

MOMBASA, Kenya — The leader of a Kenyan doomsday cult linked to the deaths of more than 400 people was sentenced on Friday to 200 years in prison for the murders of 191 people.

The High Court in Kenya's coastal city of Mombasa issued the sentence for Pastor Paul Mackenzie. He was convicted of murdering 190 children and one adult after he ordered his followers to starve themselves to death in order to meet Jesus.

Mackenzie is also facing terrorism and manslaughter charges for the more than 200 other victims, as well as child abuse and torture charges in two other courts.

Justice Diana Kavedza said that Mackenzie, leader of the Good News International Church, bore the "primary criminal culpability" for relocating his followers to a remote location and ordering them to fast to death.

Mackenzie was charged with the murders alongside 28 of his followers, including guards who enforced his fasting directives and gravediggers who helped conceal the mass graves. All denied the charges, except for one person who confessed and pleaded for leniency.

Good News International Church pastor Paul Mackenzie, center, who has been convicted on 191 murder charges, arrives alongside fellow church members as he awaits sentencing at the Mombasa High Court in Mombasa, Kenya, Friday. Brian Inganga/AP hide caption

On Oct. 19, the court found all 29 of them guilty of the murder of 191 people.

national.title: Employers added 165,000 jobs in October, soaring past expectations
national.summary: Hiring across the U.S. surged last month and unemployment dipped, a sign the job market is picking up speed.
national.body: Employers across the U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, soaring past economists' forecasts and signaling that hiring is accelerating despite headwinds such as inflation.By the numbersHiring came in much hotter than expected, with economists polled by FactSet predicting the economy added 65,000 new jobs last month. The unemployment rate stood at 4.1% in October, dipping from 4.2% in the prior month.The Labor Department on Friday also revised up payroll gains for August and September by a combined 84,000, a sign that hiring those months was more robust than previously reported.Job growth expanded across a range of sectors, led by professional and business services, which added 70,000 jobs, and health care, which added 42,000. Hiring is showing signs of revival after a sluggish 2025, when employers added an average of just 10,000 new jobs per month. Through October, payroll gains in 2026 have averaged around 86,000 a month. With corporate profits and consumer spending remaining healthy, layoffs also remain low despite stubborn inflation and recent jitters in the stock market over whether the pace of AI investment is sustainable. "Today's jobs report is a strong rebuttal to fears that the economy is heading into a meaningful slowdown," Seema Shah, chief global strategist at the investment firm Principal Asset Management, said in an email. "Payroll growth surprised firmly to the upside, unemployment fell back to 4.1% and job creation remains broad-based, pointing to an economy that is still absorbing labor comfortably rather than one beginning to buckle under tighter financial conditions."To be sure, people looking for work face challenges finding a job. The long-term unemployment rate — the share of workers who are unemployed for 27 weeks or longer — rose to 27.6% in October, from 27.1% the month prior. And labor data suggests that employers are conferring at least some roles that historically would've gone to younger Americans to artificial intelligence. local.title: Rare earths facility in Greece eyes $54 million in tax breaks and aid
local.summary: The state and local incentives do not include other private investments to help facilitate the $375 million project.
local.body:
A rare-earth facility to be built at the former Kodak Park is in line for $54.2 million in combined state and local government assistance.

Much of the package aiding Massachusetts-based Phoenix Tailings consists of tax credits and exemptions, rather than direct funding, according to the company. The total does not include investment to upgrade power infrastructure by RED-Rochester, which oversees park utilities. The railroad spur serving the 1600 Lexington Ave. facility also will require investment.

The forthcoming facility, announced last month , would cull the highly sought-after metals from mine waste and other industrial sources at an Eastman Business Park industrial warehouse complex in Greece.

Phoenix's capital outlay is estimated at $375 million, according to Gov. Kathy Hochul. But the company estimates its total costs, including needed chemicals and other operational expenses, at $600 million.

The combined public commitment, announced by Phoenix on Thursday, "underscores New York’s commitment to the project and bipartisan support for expanding U.S. production of critical materials," a company statement read.

Those rare earth metals are key in the production of electric vehicles, electronics, and defense equipment, but China currently controls most of the supply.

Local operations are scheduled to ramp up in 2027, with full production planned for 2028. The Eastman Business Park facility is projected to support 90 jobs at launch, and more than 200 when fully operational.

The company anticipates additional support for equipment purchases and workforce training through county programs.

local.title: As state moves away from Regents exams, RCSD expands career and college readiness efforts
local.summary: A new statewide framework for high school graduation requirements is in a transition period, and the Rochester City School District is making moves to meet the moment.
local.body:
Listen • 1:18 A new statewide framework for high school graduation requirements is in a transition period, and the Rochester City School District is making moves to meet the moment.

By 2029, public schools across New York will need to assess students' academic performance under the "Portrait of a Graduate" framework.

That model outlines that students must show competency in effective communication, critical thinking, creative innovation, and other academic areas.

At the Rochester City School District, Superintendent Eric Jay Rosser said the district is already shifting focus from Regents exam readiness to capstone project assessments.

"It gives us an opportunity to rethink readiness around what our students truly need for life after graduation,” he said.

Rosser created a new Department of College, Career and Civic Readiness, he said, which will keep track of student participation, and position counselors in secondary schools beginning next year.

"For me, this work comes down to making sure every student leaves us with real options, either a college of their choice, a career of their choice, with opportunities while they're in school to understand the benefits of civic engagement."

The district does not have a public-facing implementation plan for the state-mandated changes, but Rosser said he expects to get more guidance from state officials in the near future.

local.title: Inside MCH’s Friendship Place, rethinking dementia care
local.summary: Plans to redesign Friendship Place, a 25-bed secure unit, began in 2019 with the help of dementia-care expert consultants from around the world.
local.body:
Lydia Cordero had been living at Crimson Ridge Meadows, an assisted living facility, for three years when the 82-year-old started needing more support than the facility could provide.

But with widespread nursing shortages made worse by the COVID pandemic, the number of skilled nursing beds — including those for memory-care patients — has declined across the region and nationally. Her family’s top choices for local memory-care units had waitlists of up to 2 1⁄2 years, according to Lydia's daughter-in-law, Nancy Cordero.

That's when Crimson Ridge suggested the family check out Friendship Place at Monroe Community Hospital.

“When we walked in there, we fell in love with the place,” said Nancy, who toured the recently renovated facility with her husband, Miguel A. Cordero Jr.

“The courtyard was amazing,” she said. “And that's why we picked the room that we did for Mom. Mom is a people watcher, and her room looks right into the courtyard."

Friendship Place is a 25-bed secure unit for residents who may wander, including those with dementia and Alzheimer’s disease. Planning for the redesign began in 2019 — although it stalled when the pandemic hit — with the help of dementia-care expert consultants from around the world. Construction began last year, and the first residents moved in earlier this fall.

It had been decades since its last refresh, and Alyssa Tallo, executive health director at the hospital, said it was time to make some changes.

“We wanted to ... bring it up to a more home-like environment,” she said. “I think someone referred to the (previous) color scheme as ‘Pepto pink.’ It really was outdated. It was not dementia-friendly (based on) what we know now.”

local.body:
Separation anxiety was mightily apparent during a vote in Canada last month. Oil-laden Alberta, which appears more conservative in its values than the rest of the country that proudly waves the maple leaf flag, will not be on its own anytime soon.

A referendum that would have created a path toward a future election and led to possible independence for the province was defeated by a 75% to 25% margin that included more than 1.9 million votes. It is an impressive showing when considering that 5.1 million reside there.

Despite the deflating result, naysayers are not ready to give up the fight. “We’re not going anywhere,” said Jeff Rath of the Alberta Prosperity Project, the Associated Press reported. “We’ve dominated the conversation in the last year. We’ve been educating Albertans on the benefits of independence, and we’re going to continue moving forward.”

It has been a rough couple of years for our neighbors to the north. Not only is animosity brewing from within, U.S. President Donald Trump ruffled feathers by threatening to make the nation our 51st state. He then began a trade war that has harmed relations between the border nations who were once seen as being best of friends.

Retaliation, however, has been swift and painful. Many from the North are choosing to travel elsewhere, impacting tourism in parts of Western New York that include Chautauqua Institution. They're also being more global, looking to expand and grow economic partnerships with European countries.

In Canada, when the relations with the U.S. became precarious, leadership looked across the Atlantic Ocean. They kept their options open.

That brings us to the major rift within New York: upstate and downstate.

This week's election proved again that portions of rural, red-leaning regions still have very little clout in an entity that is dominated by New York City and metropolitan counties that include Erie, Monroe, Onondaga and Albany. Through an Assembly and Senate that leans far left, policies that are driven by those living downstate continue to hamper our way of life.

local.summary: As deer hunting season begins to hit its stride across Western New York, the valleys of southern Chautauqua County, particularly those near the Pennsylvania line, have already been feeling the bite of autumn. Frost-covered pumpkins and a string of chilly mornings, despite our overall warming trend,
local.body:
Submitted Photo Clint Catchot used a Mathews Lift-X bow set at 75 pounds draw weight, topped with a Grim Reaper Pro broadhead to take home this giant deer last week in Southern Chautauqua County.

Submitted Photo Big Chautauqua County deer are not new for 33-year-old Clint Catchot, who credits his Uncle Craig Silleman with getting him started in hunting when he was 12-years-old.

As deer hunting season begins to hit its stride across Western New York, the valleys of southern Chautauqua County, particularly those near the Pennsylvania line, have already been feeling the bite of autumn. Frost-covered pumpkins and a string of chilly mornings, despite our overall warming trend, signal a change in the woods. For some hunters, the early cold snaps can mean an early turn in the whitetail rut.

For 33-year-old Clint Catchot of Perrysburg, the timing couldn’t have been better. Catchot is a seasoned hunter who has already taken his share of impressive bucks, but recently experienced what every deer hunter hopes will happen someday: an encounter with the biggest buck of his life. The result was a remarkable 153-inch whitetail (estimated green score) taken from a treestand on a permission property in southern Chautauqua County.

Catchot had hung the stand just one day before the hunt. After seeing a few does and a smaller buck that first evening, he decided to return the following morning. It was a decision that would make for a hunt he won’t soon forget. The morning started with a little mishap when he dropped his grunt call and backpack from the tree. Mother Nature and the woods had other plans.

“Ten minutes later I saw a doe and a fawn. Ten minutes after that the buck came through 70 yards down wind,” Catchot recalled. The buck was moving cautiously, taking his time and seemingly checking every inch of his surroundings. He uses grunt calls from time to time.

“Very slow and cautious. He would walk 10 yards then look around for a minute or two. Then walk 10 more yards and do it again.”

It was a test of patience. With his experience, Catchot knew better than to rush the moment. Eventually, the buck worked his way to inside 35 yards, offering a broadside opportunity.

local.body:
Students from SUNY Fredonia will be doing their part to contribute to their community this weekend. Fredonia's annual Fall Sweep is this Saturday beginning around noon throughout the village.

Fall Sweep is an annual volunteer initiative where SUNY Fredonia students partner with the Village of Fredonia to assist residents with seasonal yard cleanup, leaf collection, and neighborhood beautification. The event is one of SUNY Fredonia's largest civic engagement events, bringing together hundreds of students to support local homeowners and strengthen campus-community connections.

"It's a really fun event and I really appreciate the community for letting us do this every year. It means a lot to the campus to be able to go out and do it, and I'm sure it means a lot to the community too," said Syd Smith, Chair of Community Relations through the Student Association at SUNY Fredonia.

Various student clubs participate in the event, where they are each assigned a street in the village. Homeowners in the village hang fliers on their door if they wish to participate, and on the day of the event, students stop by to rake leaves and clean the lawn. The event usually lasts roughly two hours before students meet back on campus for a reception.

Fall Sweep began roughly two decades ago. It was previously coordinated by the student-run Applied Communication Association, but last year, Smith took over coordinating the event as a freshman at Fredonia. The Applied Communication Association is assisting this year under Smith's direction.

"It was definitely a lot to handle as a freshman with not a lot of experience with the campus at all. I was kind of thrown into it, but I honestly wouldn't have had it any other way," Smith said.

Roughly 300 students participated in last year's event. Now in her second year running things, Smith hopes for another successful event this weekend with 17 clubs signed up to participate.

"We had a great turnout last year. It was amazing. I couldn't have asked for a better turnout for my first year," Smith said.

local.body:
The Patterson Library will host a special historical presentation by author Mary Ellen Humphrey at 5:30 p.m. Thursday. The discussion will focus on Mercy Otis Warren and her influential, multi-layered role before, during, and after the American Revolution, drawing from the author’s compelling book, "Corresponding With Marcia."

Warren was one of the most formidable political writers and propagandists of the Revolutionary era, utilizing her sharp wit and extensive correspondence to shape early American political thought. The presentation will explore her life, her amazing contributions to the fight for independence, and her enduring legacy as a historian of the Revolution.

“Mercy Otis Warren’s voice was vital to the foundation of American liberty, yet her full impact is often left in the shadows of the Founding Fathers,” said Mary Ellen Humphrey, author of Corresponding With Marcia. “This presentation aims to reveal her brilliant role in the Boston Tea Party, and the adoption of the Bill of Rights to our constitution, and much more. We've heard history. This is her story.”

The event is free and open to the public. It will take place in the community room at the Patterson Library, located at 40 S Portage St, Westfield, NY 14787.

For more information about the event or to reserve a seat, please visit the Patterson Library website atpattersonlib.org or call (716) 326-2154.

Humphrey is an author and educator. "Corresponding With Marcia" is the culmination of extensive research into the personal works and political influence of this woman during the American Revolution.

local.title: LIV Golf tells bankruptcy court it will wind down operations
local.summary: LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support. “The debtors are not currently proceeding with
local.body:
LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape with promise of Saudi riches, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support.

“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business.”

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable “LIV 2.0.” But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren’t interested.

“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf,” BC Partners said in a statement. “While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV -- said to be worth some $100 million -- to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players’ last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives, including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O’Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn’t going forward.

local.title: Economy growing, purchasing power is not
local.summary: The economy is strong by conventional measures, but most voters don’t feel it. Gross domestic product grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Consumer spending increased 3.8 percent, and nonresidential business investment surged 12.7 percent, propelled by artificial intell
local.body:
The economy is strong by conventional measures, but most voters don't feel it. Gross domestic product grew 3.4 percent in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year. Consumer spending increased 3.8 percent, and nonresidential business investment surged 12.7 percent, propelled by artificial intelligence and the data center build-out.

At the same time, the final Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll before the midterms found that 75 percent of Americans describe the economy as poor or not so good. Forty-eight percent say they're financially not as well off since President Donald Trump took office, more than three times the 15 percent who say they're better off. Fewer than 3 in 10 Americans approve of how Trump is handling the economy.

Democrats are favored to flip the House on Tuesday and have a real chance to capture the Senate. Persistent inflation, more than anything else, explains why the party in power is not receiving more credit for economic growth, low unemployment, deregulation, stock market gains and historic levels of capital investment.

Inflation has been a problem since Washington pumped trillions of dollars in stimulus into the economy during the covid pandemic. While inflation has cooled from its 9.1 percent peak in 2022, Trump has contributed to rising prices with unnecessary tariffs, an overzealous immigration crackdown and the Iran war, which has raised energy costs.

Inflation is a corrosive stealth tax that makes people feel like they're not getting ahead. Average hourly earnings rose 3 percent over the past year, but consumer prices climbed 3.7 percent. As a result, real hourly earnings fell 0.7 percent. Gasoline jumped 9.1 percent in September and is now 34.2 percent more expensive than a year ago.

No wonder affordability is front and center. Nearly two-thirds of campaign ads in competitive races last week mentioned the economy.

The squeeze is especially acute in districts that will determine House control. A Post analysis last week found that 6 in 10 families cannot afford the basic cost of living in the 46 most competitive districts. Between 2019 and 2024, median costs rose 33 percent while median incomes rose 28 percent. Incomes failed to keep pace with costs in 42 of the 46 districts.

Trump won in 2024 by promising relief from those pressures. Some of his policies are instead aggravating them. Take tariffs. Federal Reserve researchers found that tariffs imposed in 2025 raised core goods prices 3.1 percent through February. Yale's Budget Lab estimated that the tariffs in place over the summer would raise consumer prices about 0.7 percent, costing the average household roughly $1,100 annually.

local.summary: Steve St. George was, in fact, granted a special use permit to operate a concrete and asphalt recycling yard at a property he owns in the town. At the third Zoning Board hearing regarding the project, held in October, the Board granted the permit with a list of conditions attached. A previous OBSERV
local.body:
Steve St. George was, in fact, granted a special use permit to operate a concrete and asphalt recycling yard at a property he owns in the town. At the third Zoning Board hearing regarding the project, held in October, the Board granted the permit with a list of conditions attached.

A previous OBSERVER article erroneously reported the project was still awaiting approval, citing Zoning Board discussions held in October 2025 -- the first of three hearings -- rather than the most recent discussions held in October 2026, as the project received approval.

On Oct. 6, the Town of Pomfret Zoning Board of Appeals granted St. George a special use permit for recycling operations at 3624 Webster Road, Fredonia. The property was formerly used for grape vineyards.

St. George operates S. St. George Enterprises, a construction company that often works with roadways in the region. St. George sought a permit to recycle the materials from his company on site. Initially, a building permit at the site was denied because the use was not defined under the zoning code's acceptable uses.

Members of the Zoning Board recently conducted a site visit, during which the equipment was run at full speed and volume. The decibels were measured and the readings did not pass the threshold to require ear protection. Chairman David Fridmann spoke with the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), who provided documentation that authorized the operations until 2031. The DEC will continue to monitor the project.

The Zoning Board was required to evaluate the project under the State Environmental Quality Review Act guidelines. The Board issued a negative declaration, meaning that the project does not negatively impact the environment.

In granting St. George approval, the Zoning Board restricted operation of recycling equipment to weekdays between 7:30 a.m. and 4 p.m., aside from delivery or transport from the site. Operation of recycling equipment is restricted to 50 days annually. If the operations grow in scale to require more than 50 days annually, another special use permit application must be filed.

The September hearing featured objections from roughly a dozen residents in attendance from the community neighboring the site. Residents shared concerns with noise, dust, well water contamination, hours of operation, and lighting. The Board also highlighted concerns with environmental impacts.

local.summary: Buffalo City Hall could be getting a $200 million makeover as officials pursue National Historic Landmark status to help fund the restoration.
local.body: Buffalo's iconic City Hall is set for a major makeover, with plans for more than $200 million worth of improvements over the next five to eight years, along with the pursuit of National Historic Landmark status to help fund the project. local.title: Restoration of Our Lady of Victory Basilica dome nears completion in Lackawanna
local.summary: Crews are nearing the final stages of restoration work on the iconic dome of the Basilica of Our Lady of Victory in Lackawanna.
local.body: Crews are nearing the final stages of restoration work on the iconic dome of the Basilica of Our Lady of Victory in Lackawanna.Monsignor David LiPuma said the restoration is nearly 80% finished, with fall weather allowing crews to make headway before winter."It's been beautiful," Monsignor LiPuma said. "It's been a great fall, which means that we can really move along on restoring that beautiful dome."One of the latest developments involves the cupola, the structure atop the dome. Crews are preparing to remove its copper and install a protective covering for the winter months.Monsignor LiPuma said the temporary covering allows the team to monitor how it performs through the winter before returning in the spring to replace the copper and continue work on the dome.WATCH: Restoration of Our Lady of Victory Basilica dome nears completion in LackawannaCrews are expected to continue working in December, weather permitting, before taking a winter break.The current timeline calls for the restoration, including the cupola, to be completed in July 2027. All scaffolding is expected to come down in August, allowing visitors and passersby to see the restored dome in its entirety."If the weather continues and things move along, by the end of July, we should have the dome completed with the cupola and by the end of August, all the scaffolding will be down, and we'll be able to see it in its entirety," Monsignor LiPuma said.The project is part of a broader effort to preserve one of Western New York's most recognizable religious and architectural landmarks.Monsignor LiPuma said the restoration is about ensuring the dome is part of the region's landscape for generations to come."It's amazing that, at this time in history, we can restore it for the next 100 years because it lasted 100 years; that copper dome lasted 100 years," Monsignor LiPuma said.

Parke’s latest inevitably viral launch comes in the form of a collaboration with beloved accessories brand Stoney Clover Lane .

The limited-edition drop, available on both Parke’s website and Stoney Clover Lane’s website on Friday, Nov. 6, is chock-full of each brand’s customer favorites: denim, duffels, pouches, bag charms and, of course, a reimagined version of Parke’s signature Varsity Mockneck .

entertainment.title: Anuel AA Talks Corridos Era, Fuerza Regida Collab & Posts About Ex Karol G: ‘Maybe She’ll Unblock Me’
entertainment.summary: The Puerto Rican superstar previews Real Hasta la Muerte 2 and Cartel Real Hasta la Muerte . Watch the full interview here.
entertainment.body:
Anuel AA has plenty to talk about, from the recent changes he’s made in his life to his move into Mexican corridos — and his playful jokes about his ex, Colombian superstar Karol G . In an interview with Billboard ‘s co-chief content officer Leila Cobo, released Friday (Nov. 6), aboard a yacht in Miami, he also explains why he’s fallen in love with music all over again.

The Puerto Rican trap star says he decided about six months ago to stop smoking and drinking, and that he feels more alert now. “You mature over time, you know what I mean? And life teaches you things,” he admits. “Drugs don’t fulfill you, fame doesn’t fulfill you, money doesn’t fulfill you.”

That change comes amid a busy stretch for his music. Anuel says Real Hasta la Muerte 2 is coming Nov. 19, and he may also release Cartel Real Hasta la Muerte — a Mexican corridos album he’s still finishing — on the same day. Exploring the genre has meant learning a different way to sing and working with Mexican musicians. “I fell in love with music all over again — with something new, not the same old thing,” he says.

“There are going to be songs produced by Fuerza Regida. I’m talking with Jesús [Ortiz Paz] — he’s my brother, and he’s helping me with a few songs,” he adds.

The conversation also touches on his kids, business ventures and relationships with his exes. When Cobo asks if he asked Karol G to unblock him on social media, Anuel laughs: “No, I’m just messing with her. But maybe she’ll unblock me.”

“Do you want all your exes to be at peace with you?” Cobo asks. “Well, not all of them — not my ex… We should live in peace, right?” he replies. The exchange stays playful, and Anuel jokes that a movie about his love life would be called Los Amores perros de Anuel (or Anuel’s Love’s a B–ch ): “It’ll sell a lot. It’ll be incredible.”

Between news about his upcoming projects and personal revelations, the interview offers a look at Anuel as he rethinks his life and music. Watch the full conversation above.

On Nov. 19, Anuel AA will release Real Hasta la Muerte 2 , a tribute to the original Real Hasta la Muerte , alongside his first corridos album, Cartel Real Hasta la Muerte .

The rapper also shares that Karol G still hasn’t unblocked him on social media and how he made peace with fellow rapper Cosculluela. He opens up about his sobriety, and how during his darkest moments, he couldn’t recognize himself in the mirror. Today, he’s celebrating new collaborations with Fuerza Regida and Luis R Conriquez, as well as his love for Mexican culture. He also talks about how much he loves his children, why De La Rose is like “Anuel in a woman’s body,” Puerto Rico, and the new music festival he’ll launch in 2027.

entertainment.title: Olivia Dean, Kehlani, Juanes & More to Announce 2027 Grammy Nominations
entertainment.summary: And heads-up: The 2027 Grammys will air/stream at 4 p.m. PT, one hour earlier than before.
entertainment.body:
Olivia Dean , the reigning Grammy winner for best new artist, is widely expected to receive multiple Grammy nominations, including album, record and song of the year, on Monday Nov. 16. She’s also set to help announce the nominations on a livestream bright and early that morning, along with Kehlani , who won two Grammys earlier this year and could be in line for more awards for her eponymous album; Amy Allen , who has won songwriter of the year, non-classical the last two years; and Pharrell Williams , a past three-time winner of producer of the year, non-classical.

Other artists set for the nominations livestream include Alan Menken, Carly Pearce, David Guetta, FYÜTCH & Aura V, Herbie Hancock, Israel Houghton, Juanes, Linda Perry, Meghan Foley & Michelle Holme, Renée Fleming, YUNGBLUD and Ziggy Marley, as well as Harvey Mason jr., Grammys CEO, and Dr. Chelsey Green, chair of the Recording Academy Board of Trustees.

Nominees across all 100 categories for the 2027 Grammys will be revealed during a special presentation on Grammy.com and the Grammys YouTube channel, with special live coverage on Good Morning America . The nominations livestream begins on Monday, Nov. 16 at 7:45 a.m. ET / 4:45 a.m. PT. There will be a wrap-up show at 9 a.m. ET/6 a.m. PT (times approximate).

For the first time, the Grammy Nominations special presentation will be broadcast live at The Square in Times Square, presented by Hilton.

The complete nominations list will be published on Grammy.com and at Billboard.com at 9:00 a.m. ET / 6:00 a.m. PT.

The Grammys also made an important announcement about the 2027 Grammys, which will air one hour earlier than in the past. The 69th annual Grammy Awards will air/stream live on Sunday Feb. 7, 2027 at 7:00 p.m. ET / 4:00 p.m. PT on ABC, and stream on Disney+ and Hulu.

This follows the lead of the Oscars, which first moved up their show to start at 4 p.m. PT for the 96th Academy Awards in 2024. The move is designed to allow viewers on the East Coast to remain with the show for the top awards without having to stay up to midnight. 2024 was Raj Kapoor’s first year as an executive producer of the Oscars. Kapoor is also an executive producer of the Grammys.

The 2027 Grammys will again be held at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles.

entertainment.title: ‘Nobody Wants This’ Renewed for Season 4 at Netflix
entertainment.summary: The Kristen Bell and Adam Brody-led rom-com will return after delivering Netflix's biggest opening week for a returning comedy series this year.
entertainment.body:
Logo text Netflix has renewed Nobody Wants This for a fourth season, The Hollywood Reporter has learned.

The renewal comes just two weeks after the release of the hit rom-com’s third season , which delivered the largest opening week for a returning comedy series on the streamer this year. Created by Erin Foster and starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody , the series accumulated 13.4 million views in its first two weeks.

“We are so happy and thrilled to do another season of our favorite show on television, which coincidentally is the one we run,” co-showrunners and executive producers Foster, Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan said in a statement. Related Stories Business Netflix Taps Mattel's Roberto Stanichi to Lead Consumer Products and Experiences TV Streaming Ratings: 'From' Netflix Effects Its Way to Top of the Charts

Season three saw major developments for central couple Joanne (Bell) and Rabbi Noah (Brody), who moved in together as they continued navigating their interfaith relationship. The season also further explored the complicated dynamics between Morgan (Justine Lupe), Sasha (Timothy Simons) and Esther (Jackie Tohn), with the latter two thrust back into the dating world following their separation at the end of season two. (Find out the full spoilers for what happened in Nobody Wants This season three here .)

The season three cast also included Stephanie Faracy, Michael Hitchcock, Paul Ben-Victor, Tovah Feldshuh, Andrew Rannells, Sarah Silverman, Shiloh Bearman and Sherry Cola.

The renewal comes amid recent headlines surrounding Brody’s comments about the war in Gaza. In a recent interview with GQ , the actor said, “Put me down as thinking it’s a genocide. Put me down as wanting a free Palestine.” He added, “It’s awful that it’s taken so much death and misery, but it does feel like it’s reaching a breaking point that it should have a while ago.”

Following Brody’s comments, Rabbi Steve Leder, the former senior rabbi of Wilshire Boulevard Temple in Los Angeles — where Foster converted to Judaism — and a technical adviser on the show’s first season, criticized the actor .

“You by your own admission, are a relatively ignorant Jew, and your ignorance really showed the other day. Here’s some technical advice: If you know nothing about something, you should say nothing about it,” Leder said.

entertainment.title: P1Harmony Say It’s Never Too Late to ‘BLOW UP,’ Citing Charli xcx As Inspiration
entertainment.summary: The six-piece say they're ready to BLOW UP with a new hyperpop single after navigating compromise, career pressures and getting their label to listen.
entertainment.body:
During P1Harmony ‘s first six years together, there was a stretch when members couldn’t articulate why they were working so hard.

“What I felt was hardest in this process was when I couldn’t find a reason for running,” Intak tells Billboard during a sit-down in their downtown Los Angeles hotel hours before they fly home to Seoul. “There were times the company just had us run without a clear purpose or a point to reach and I think I got a little worn out the moment I realized that. ‘What is our purpose in this moment? What are we running this hard for? Is it even true that running like this will get us there?’ Every time I had moments like that, I’d suddenly feel drained and it was hard. But even if our steps were really small, we always climbed little by little.”

Six years into their career, the six-piece of Intak, Keeho, Theo, Jiung, Soul and Jongseob has a much clearer view of where all that running is taking them. The K-pop act’s newest EP BLOW UP arrived Friday (Nov. 6), and its title doubles as a mantra for where the group stands today. After years of steady gains on the charts, in album sales, in concert audiences and in hard-won lessons inside the boy band, they’re ready to break through in a bigger way. Related Queens of the Stone Age Crowned on ARIA Chart With 'Perfecth' Lil Baby Brings 'Fresh' to Life: Stream It Now Lil Baby, JENNIE, Dove Cameron, XG, Boys Noize & More: New Music Friday Guide Explore P1Harmony See latest videos, charts and news

P1Harmony’s performance at 82WORLD: LA , their first headlining slot at a U.S. festival the previous weekend, felt like proof. “The last time we did an outdoor thing was the first time we came to L.A.,” leader Keeho recollects. “It’s been like almost four to five years and that’s a really big, full-circle moment.”

Numbers show how far that gratitude goes, with Intak saying he can track the group’s progress in chart positions. “Before, our goal was just to get onto Billboard ,” he says. “Just the other day we were at No. 60, then we’re getting into the top 20 and now the top 5. Because we achieved these things one by one, I feel reassured now and I think it’s good that we can show our fans we’re artists who can do at least this much.”

P1H’s six albums’ worth of Billboard 200 history — all EPs — show just that: After first entering the chart at No. 51 with HARMONY : ALL IN during the summer of 2023, P1Harmony earned their first top 40 album with 2024’s Killin’ It (No. 39 peak), followed by SAD SONG (No. 16 in 2024), DUH! (No. 23 in 2025) and their debut English-language EP, EX (No. 9, their first Top 10 in fall 2025). Earlier this year, UNIQUE debuted at No. 4 on the Billboard 200 , the group’s best showing yet, earning 58,000 equivalent album units in its first week.
